Kkakdugi Radish Kimchi

Kkakdugi is baechu kimchi's (#B01) radish sibling: the same paste, cubed Korean radish instead of cabbage, a faster ferment, and a crunch that survives weeks longer.

Korean · Medium · Makes about 1.5 kg

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: heritage — the kimchi that matches the stew pots. Kkakdugi is baechu kimchi's (#B01) radish sibling: the same paste, cubed Korean radish instead of cabbage, a faster ferment, and a crunch that survives weeks longer. At the grill table it is the bowl that loves the braised and stewed records — the jangjorim (#B20), the oily fish (#SF07) — because radish's clean, peppery snap cuts richness the way cabbage's leaves cannot. If you have made B01, you have already made this paste; this record is the cube law and the radish clock.

The radish and the salt
The paste (the B01 family recipe)

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Cube evenly — the cube is the recipe's clock. 2.5 cm cubes salt and ferment at the same rate; a batch mixed with half-cubes and whole chunks ferments unevenly (the small cubes go sour while the large ones stay raw). Weigh your knife discipline here, not your ingredients.
  • Salt the cubes 30 minutes, loose in a bowl, turning once. The radish weeps a brine and its corners soften a half-step. Save 2 tablespoons of the wept brine for the paste; drain the rest.
  • Make the paste while the cubes drain: everything above whisked to a rust slurry, scallions last.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    The drained cubes and the paste folded together with your hands until every cube wears a coat and the bowl runs deep red-orange. Checkpoint — taste a pasted cube raw: salty, savory-hot, the radish's sweet pepper under it. This is day zero — the flavor that ferments into the bowl.
  2. 02
    Pack into a clean jar with 3 cm of headspace, pressed to squeeze out air, weight on top, loose lid — B01's entire packing law, unchanged. Checkpoint — brine rises over the cubes within a day (top up with the saved brine or salted water if it lags — under-liquid is the safety architecture, same as the cabbage).
  3. 03
    Ferment at cool room temperature 1–2 days (radish runs faster than cabbage — its sugars are more available) until the brine fizzes faintly and the sourness arrives, then refrigerate. Checkpoint — day-two taste: the cube snaps audibly, the paste's heat has rounded, a clean sour line on the finish. Kkakdugi's window from young-crunchy to complex-sour is weeks in the fridge, and its snap outlives cabbage's by a wide margin. Chef’s Note — kkakdugi's brine is famous in its own right: cold, cloudy, spicy-sour, it is the traditional ladle into kongguksu and cold noodle soups, and the smart batch is packed a little wetter than instinct says for exactly that reason. Pour a shot of it over the day-after fried rice (#M10's leftovers) and the jar has now seasoned three meals.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Cubes fermented unevenlyMixed cube sizesEven 2.5 cm; no halves
Brine never coveredUnder-salted cubesTop up with saved brine
Too saltyRadish over-drainedA rinse at packing; keep more pear in the paste
Soft cubesWarm ferment too longFridge at first fizz; radish wants the short room stage

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Refrigerated, honestly good a month — radish's crunch holds longer than cabbage's. The brine keeps serving (see Note) until the jar is empty.
  • Variations: the cabbage parent (#B01); cubed Asian pear folded in at packing (the palace style, sweet bursts); the same paste on cucumber runs #B03 at its faster clock.
